title: Dishwasher: get the pump, heater, valves and stainless tub
summary: A dishwasher gives you two water pumps (circulation and drain), a heating element of about 1 kW, a mains water inlet valve, sensors, a control board and a stainless-steel tub. Allow about an hour. It runs on mains and is often hardwired under the counter, so isolate it at the breaker and prove it dead first; it is also heavy and full of sharp sheet metal.

steps.text: Isolate it. Most dishwashers plug in under the sink or are hardwired to a junction box behind the kick plate. Switch off its breaker and tape it off, then check the supply wires with a meter before you touch any of them (see safety_mains_isolation). If it plugs in, unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it.
steps.warn: A wrong breaker or a second feed can leave the wires live. Meter them dead first.

steps.text: Shut off the water at the small valve under the sink. Put a tray under the inlet fitting and unscrew the supply line. Pull the drain hose off the sink trap or disposal (it is clamped on) and let it run out into a bucket.

Free the machine. Undo the brackets that hold it to the underside of the counter (usually two screws at the top front) and adjust the front feet so it clears the floor. Slide it out on cardboard, keeping the hoses and cable clear. Tip it back and drain the sump: expect a litre or two of dirty water.
steps.warn: A dishwasher weighs 35–50 kg and tips forward when you pull it out with the door open. Use a helper and keep your feet clear.

steps.text: Take off the kick plate (2–4 screws) and the lower front panel. The inlet valve, pumps and low hoses are all in this space. Photograph the wiring, then unplug each connector one at a time by pressing its latch. Do not pull on the wires.

Inlet valve: it is a small plastic block with a coil on top, behind the kick plate on one side. Squeeze the hose clamp with pliers and pull the outlet hose off, undo the two mounting screws, unscrew the supply fitting and unplug the two-wire coil.

Pumps: they sit in the sump at the bottom of the tub. Squeeze the hose clamps and pull the hoses off, then release the pump from its mount (screws, or a quarter-turn twist lock) and lower it. Some come out from the front; others only from underneath, so lay the machine on its back on cardboard with a helper. Machines with a combined pump keep both in one housing: take it whole.

Heating element: most machines have a bare U-shaped element on the tub floor, held by two nuts and unplugged by two spade terminals underneath. Pull the spades, undo the nuts and lift it up out of the tub from inside. Newer machines with a flow-through heater built into the pump housing have no loose element: leave it attached to the pump.
Sensors: the temperature sensor (a small thermistor) and the turbidity or water-level sensors sit in or beside the sump. Unplug them and cut the wires 10 cm back from each connector.

Control board: the board lives in the door behind the control panel. Remove the screws along the inner edge of the door and lift the outer panel off. Unplug the harness plugs and release the board from its clips. Leave the door hinges, cables and springs alone.
steps.warn: Door balance springs and cables are under heavy tension and lash out if released. Never unhook them.

steps.text: Tub: with the parts out, lay the shell on its back and unscrew the tub from the outer frame, or cut the case away from it. A pressed stainless tub is one piece, usually 50–70 litres. Check it with a magnet: plastic and enamelled tubs are not worth keeping.
steps.warn: Cut and torn stainless edges slice skin. Wear gloves and eye protection and fold sharp edges over.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Circulation pump.** A mains motor and impeller that moves a lot of water at low pressure but cannot lift it more than a couple of metres. Good for circulating water through a rain-tank filter, flushing or shifting water between tanks.
- **Drain pump.** A smaller pump that lifts roughly a metre. Good for emptying tanks, sumps and grey water. Neither pump is made for drinking-water duty: both have seen detergent and food, and neither should run dry for long.
- **Heating element.** A sheathed mains heater, commonly 800–2,000 W. Fit it into a water tank as an immersion heater (with a thermostat, a fuse and a protective earth), or into a drying box or small oven. Keep it clear of plastic.
- **Inlet valve.** A solenoid valve with a mains-voltage coil. Use it to fill a tank under float-switch control. Read its label for the minimum water pressure it needs to open.
- **Sensors.** The thermistor makes a thermometer or thermostat input. The turbidity sensor is an LED and photo-detector pair in a small housing.
- **Control board.** Usually several relays (10–16 A) and a triac or two, plus connectors and a microcontroller. Worth taking for the relays.
- **Stainless tub.** A food-safe stainless shell: use it as a water tank, a smoker or oven body, a solar dehydrator box or a charcoal retort.
- **Racks.** The vinyl-coated wire baskets make drying racks and shelves.

## Using the mains parts

Every motor, heater and valve here wants 120 V or 230 V AC, so they need a generator or an inverter. Power them through a fuse, never from a bare lead.

## Variations

- Portable countertop models are smaller but hold the same parts.
- Older machines have a cam timer (a small motor turning cams) instead of a board.
- Some machines have a salt container for a water softener; keep the salt.

## What to leave

- The spray arms, door gaskets and plastic racks that have cracked.
- The sound-deadening blanket around the tub: it may be glass fibre. Skip it, or wear gloves and a mask.
- The door, hinges and springs.
